claim: Schistosomiasis affects over 230 million people.
source: Schistosomiasis (infection with parasitic blood flukes) affects over 230 million people, with severe infections causing ~200,000 deaths per year.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the introduction providing epidemiological data about schistosomiasis prevalence.

claim: Severe schistosomiasis infections cause approximately 200,000 deaths per year.
source: Schistosomiasis (infection with parasitic blood flukes) affects over 230 million people, with severe infections causing ~200,000 deaths per year.
evidence: This is a direct statement providing mortality statistics for schistosomiasis.

claim: Chronic schistosomiasis infections are associated with anemia, impaired cognitive development and stunted growth.
source: Chronic infections are associated with morbidities such as anemia, impaired cognitive development and stunted growth (Colley et al., 2014; King and Dangerfield-Cha, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Schistosomiasis infection is acquired upon exposure to freshwater larval cercariae which penetrate the host skin.
source: Infection is acquired upon exposure to freshwater, larval cercariae which penetrate the host skin.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of infection transmission.

claim: Inside host tissue, cercariae transform into schistosomula that access and traverse the circulatory system, pass through the lungs and liver before finally residing as mature adults within either the mesenteric vessels or vasculature surrounding the urinary bladder.
source: Inside host tissue, cercariae transform into schistosomula that access and traverse the circulatory system, pass through the lungs and liver before finally residing as mature adults within either the mesenteric vessels (Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum) or vasculature surrounding the urinary bladder (Schistosoma haematobium) (Wilson, 2009; Georgi et al., 1986).
evidence: This describes the parasite life cycle within the host, supported by citations.

claim: Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum reside as mature adults within the mesenteric vessels.
source: Inside host tissue, cercariae transform into schistosomula that access and traverse the circulatory system, pass through the lungs and liver before finally residing as mature adults within either the mesenteric vessels (Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum) or vasculature surrounding the urinary bladder (Schistosoma haematobium) (Wilson, 2009; Georgi et al., 1986).
evidence: This specifies the anatomical location of specific schistosome species.

claim: Schistosoma haematobium resides as mature adults within vasculature surrounding the urinary bladder.
source: Inside host tissue, cercariae transform into schistosomula that access and traverse the circulatory system, pass through the lungs and liver before finally residing as mature adults within either the mesenteric vessels (Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum) or vasculature surrounding the urinary bladder (Schistosoma haematobium) (Wilson, 2009; Georgi et al., 1986).
evidence: This specifies the anatomical location of S. haematobium.

claim: Sexually mature male and female schistosome worms pair up and generate hundreds to thousands of eggs per female worm per day.
source: The sexually mature male and female worms pair up and generate a prodigious number of eggs, depositing hundreds to thousands of eggs per female worm per day (Cheever, 1969; Cheever et al., 1994; Barlow and Meleney, 1949).
evidence: This describes the reproductive output of schistosomes, supported by citations.

claim: Schistosome eggs lodge within peritoneal organs, evoking a massive Th2 response which cues granuloma formation and consequent pathology in affected organs.
source: Eggs lodge within the peritoneal organs, evoking a massive Th2 response which cues granuloma formation and consequent pathology in affected organs (reviewed in [Cheever, 1969]).
evidence: This describes the immunopathological response to schistosome eggs, supported by citation.

claim: In urogenital schistosomiasis, eggs are deposited in the bladder mucosa and urinary tract, resulting in hematuria and increased rates of squamous-cell carcinoma.
source: In the case of urogenital schistosomiasis (S. haematobium infection) eggs are deposited in the bladder mucosa and urinary tract, resulting in hematuria and increased rates of squamous-cell carcinoma.
evidence: This describes the pathological consequences of S. haematobium infection.

claim: In intestinal schistosomiasis, eggs are deposited in the liver and hepatic portal system leading to periportal fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension and ascites.
source: In the case of intestinal schistosomiasis (S. mansoni and S. japonicum infections), eggs are deposited in the liver and hepatic portal system leading to periportal fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension and ascites.
evidence: This describes the pathological consequences of S. mansoni and S. japonicum infections.

claim: Praziquantel has been in clinical use for nearly 40 years.
source: Broad spectrum chemotherapy of schistosomiasis relies upon praziquantel (PZQ), which has been in clinical use for nearly 40 years (Colley et al., 2014; King and Dangerfield-Cha, 2008; Andrews et al., 1983).
evidence: This provides historical context for praziquantel use, supported by citations.

claim: Mass drug administration programs will require approximately 250 million tablets of praziquantel per year for at risk populations.
source: Mass drug administration (MDA) programs will require ~250 million tablets of PZQ per year for at risk populations (Osakunor et al., 2018).
evidence: This quantifies the scale of praziquantel distribution needs, supported by citation.

claim: Praziquantel can be subcurative in areas of high intensity of infection and transmission.
source: The widespread distribution of schistosomiasis, coupled with observations that PZQ can be subcurative in areas of high intensity of infection and transmission (Danso-Appiah and De Vlas, 2002; King et al., 2011) raise concerns that treatment resistant parasites may emerge (Fallon and Doenhoff, 1994; Fallon et al., 1995; Ismail et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes limitations of praziquantel efficacy, supported by citations.

claim: There are concerns that treatment resistant schistosome parasites may emerge.
source: The widespread distribution of schistosomiasis, coupled with observations that PZQ can be subcurative in areas of high intensity of infection and transmission (Danso-Appiah and De Vlas, 2002; King et al., 2011) raise concerns that treatment resistant parasites may emerge (Fallon and Doenhoff, 1994; Fallon et al., 1995; Ismail et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This expresses concerns about drug resistance, supported by citations.

claim: Targeting parasite neuromuscular physiology has proven to be a highly successful anthelmintic approach.
source: In this regard, targeting parasite neuromuscular physiology has proven to be a highly successful anthelmintic approach (Geary et al., 1992).
evidence: This describes a general anthelmintic strategy, supported by citation.

claim: In schistosomes, serotonin controls motor function.
source: In schistosomes, serotonin (5-HT) controls motor function and a specific serotonergic G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) mediating this effect has been implicated by both RNAi (Patocka et al., 2014) and drug screening (Chan et al., 2016a, 2016b).
evidence: This describes the role of serotonin in schistosomes, supported by citations.

claim: A specific serotonergic GPCR mediating motor function in schistosomes has been implicated by both RNAi and drug screening.
source: In schistosomes, serotonin (5-HT) controls motor function and a specific serotonergic G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) mediating this effect has been implicated by both RNAi (Patocka et al., 2014) and drug screening (Chan et al., 2016a, 2016b).
evidence: This describes evidence for a specific GPCR target, supported by citations.

claim: Full-length 5-HT receptor sequences were cloned from each of three major schistosome species causing human infection worldwide.
source: Here, we cloned full-length 5-HT receptor sequences from each of three major species causing human infection worldwide and expressed these targets in a high-throughput capable assay enabling screening of thousands of compounds from natural product libraries.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The three schistosome 5-HTRs shared high amino acid similarity (84–94%).
source: The three 5HTRs shared high amino acid similarity (84–94%), and clustered with 5-HT7 receptors from other organisms (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This quantifies the sequence similarity between the cloned receptors, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The three schistosome 5-HTRs clustered with 5-HT7 receptors from other organisms.
source: The three 5HTRs shared high amino acid similarity (84–94%), and clustered with 5-HT7 receptors from other organisms (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This describes phylogenetic analysis results shown in supplementary figures.

claim: GFP-tagged variants of each schistosome 5-HTR localized at the cell surface in mammalian HEK293 cells.
source: In mammalian HEK293 cells, GFP-tagged variants of each 5-HTR localized at the cell surface (Figure 1A), enabling functional profiling.
evidence: This describes the subcellular localization of the expressed receptors, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The choice of the GloSensor cAMP reporter was guided by prior evidence demonstrating coupling of the flatworm SER-7 GPCRs to Gs.
source: The choice of this reporter was guided by prior evidence demonstrating coupling of the flatworm SER-7 GPCRs to Gs (Patocka et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2016b, 2016c) and the ability of this approach to resolve real time kinetics of cAMP generation with high sensitivity in intact cells.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the assay choice, supported by citations.

claim: Each of the schistosome 5-HTRs responded to the addition of 5-HT with a rapid elevation in luminescence values (~70–110 fold increase).
source: The 5-HTRs from each individual schistosome species were transiently transfected into a stable HEK293 cell line expressing the cAMP reporter and luminescence values monitored during addition of 5-HT. Each of the GPCRs responded to the addition of 5-HT with a rapid elevation in luminescence values (~70–110 fold increase, Figure 1C) with sensitivity in the low nanomolar range for Sj.5HTR and Sh.5HTR (EC50 = 3.0 ± 0.3, 3.6 ± 0.3 nM) and 76 ± 1 nM for Sm.5HTRL (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the functional response of the receptors to serotonin, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sj.5HTR and Sh.5HTR have sensitivity to 5-HT in the low nanomolar range (EC50 = 3.0 ± 0.3, 3.6 ± 0.3 nM).
source: The 5-HTRs from each individual schistosome species were transiently transfected into a stable HEK293 cell line expressing the cAMP reporter and luminescence values monitored during addition of 5-HT. Each of the GPCRs responded to the addition of 5-HT with a rapid elevation in luminescence values (~70–110 fold increase, Figure 1C) with sensitivity in the low nanomolar range for Sj.5HTR and Sh.5HTR (EC50 = 3.0 ± 0.3, 3.6 ± 0.3 nM) and 76 ± 1 nM for Sm.5HTRL (Figure 1D).
evidence: This quantifies the potency of 5-HT at specific receptors, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Sm.5HTRL has an EC50 for 5-HT of 76 ± 1 nM.
source: The 5-HTRs from each individual schistosome species were transiently transfected into a stable HEK293 cell line expressing the cAMP reporter and luminescence values monitored during addition of 5-HT. Each of the GPCRs responded to the addition of 5-HT with a rapid elevation in luminescence values (~70–110 fold increase, Figure 1C) with sensitivity in the low nanomolar range for Sj.5HTR and Sh.5HTR (EC50 = 3.0 ± 0.3, 3.6 ± 0.3 nM) and 76 ± 1 nM for Sm.5HTRL (Figure 1D).
evidence: This quantifies the potency of 5-HT at Sm.5HTRL, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Bromocriptine is a known antagonist of Sm.5HTRL.
source: Conditions were iterated to deliver robust resolution of the signals elicited by 5-HT ('agonist screen', Z' score >0.7, signal window >10) and the known inhibitory action of bromocriptine ('antagonist screen', Z' score >0.6, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), a previously identified antagonist (Chan et al., 2016b).
evidence: This identifies bromocriptine as a known antagonist, supported by citation.

claim: A screen of 4288 compounds from natural product libraries was performed against S. mansoni 5HTRL.
source: Having optimized these methods, we proceeded to screen the S. mansoni 5HTRL against a compilation of natural product libraries (4288 compounds, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the scale of the screening campaign.

claim: The screening dataset yielded 52 compounds (12 agonists and 40 antagonists at Sm.5HTRL, ~1.2% hit rate).
source: Overall, the screening dataset yielded 52 compounds (12 agonists and 40 antagonists at Sm.5HTRL, ~1.2% hit rate) for subsequent investigation.
evidence: This summarizes the screening results.

claim: Chemotype analysis of the hit compounds revealed two main groups of favored structures: benzylisoquinolines and compounds containing an indole ring system.
source: Chemotype analysis of the 'hit' compounds (Figure 2E) revealed two main groups of favored structures. The first core group of ligands were benzylisoquinolines with aporphine or protoberberine cores. These compounds were exclusively antagonists. The second group of compounds contained an indole ring system, either bicyclic tryptamines, or ergot alkaloids with a four ring ergoline core.
evidence: This describes the structural analysis of screening hits, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Benzylisoquinoline compounds were exclusively antagonists at Sm.5HTRL.
source: The first core group of ligands were benzylisoquinolines with aporphine or protoberberine cores. These compounds were exclusively antagonists.
evidence: This describes the pharmacological profile of a specific chemotype.

claim: Indole-containing compounds comprised both agonist and antagonist ligands at Sm.5HTRL.
source: The second group of compounds contained an indole ring system, either bicyclic tryptamines, or ergot alkaloids with a four ring ergoline core. This second group of compounds comprised both agonist and antagonist ligands.
evidence: This describes the pharmacological diversity of indole-containing compounds.

claim: Ergot alkaloids have a long history of therapeutic use.
source: Ergot alkaloids are a diverse group of compounds with a long history of therapeutic use.
evidence: This provides historical context for ergot alkaloids.

claim: Ergot alkaloid interactions with mammalian bioaminergic GPCRs encompass a range of activities and kinetic profiles.
source: Their interaction with mammalian bioaminergic GPCRs encompasses a range of activities and kinetic profiles (Knight et al., 2009; Wacker et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the pharmacological properties of ergot alkaloids, supported by citations.

claim: Complete dose-response relationships were performed for twenty ergot alkaloid compounds against all three schistosome 5-HTRs.
source: Complete dose-response relationships were performed for twenty compounds containing the tetracyclic ergoline skeleton (5 compounds from the primary screen plus 15 commercially sourced ligands) against all three schistosome 5.HTRs (Sm.5HTRL, Sh.5HTR and Sj.5HTR).
evidence: This describes the structure-activity relationship study.

claim: Ergot alkaloid interactions with the schistosome 5-HTRs spanned a range of effects including full agonists, partial agonists, antagonists and inactive compounds.
source: Second, the data evidence a broad spectrum of potencies and efficacies within the ergot alkaloid series evidencing full agonists (for example, compound '1' ergotamine, '2' dihydroergotamine), partial agonists (compound '3', lisuride), antagonists (compounds '16' terguride, '19', bromocriptine, '20' 2-bromo-LSD) as well as closely related 'inactive' compounds (compound '14', α-ergocryptine).
evidence: This summarizes the diversity of pharmacological profiles observed.

claim: The three schistosome 5-HTRs showed shared responsiveness to tested ergot alkaloid ligands.
source: First, these representations convey a shared responsiveness across the three 5-HTRs to tested ligands, suggesting a conservation of pharmacological profile between the 5-HTR orthologs from the different schistosome species.
evidence: This describes the conservation of pharmacological properties across species.

claim: Hydrogenation of the D9-10 double bond of lisuride eliminated efficacy to yield the antagonist terguride (IC50 = 400 ± 50 nM).
source: For example, hydrogenation of the D9-10 double bond of lisuride (compound '3') eliminated efficacy to yield the antagonist terguride (compound '16', IC50 = 400 ± 50 nM, Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes a specific structure-activity relationship, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Bromination of LSD at the B2 indol ring position converts the partial agonist into a potent antagonist (2-Bromo-LSD, IC50 = 100 ± 20 nM).
source: The partial agonist LSD (compound '6') is converted into a potent antagonist (IC50 = 100 ± 20 nM) on bromination at the B2 indol ring position (2-Bromo-LSD, compound '20').
evidence: This describes another specific structure-activity relationship.

claim: Ergotamine is a potent full agonist at each schistosome receptor (Emax 95 ± 4, 96 ± 5 and 114 ± 3% of 5-HT for Sm.5HTRL, Sh.5HTR and Sj.5HTR, respectively).
source: Distinct structural modifications impacting efficacy could be seen in an ergopeptine series (Figure 3D), through comparison of the chemical structures of ergotamine (compound '1'), a potent full agonist at each schistosome receptor (Emax95 ± 4, 96 ± 5 and 114 ± 3% of 5-HT for Sm.5HTRL, Sh.5HTR and Sj.5HTR, respectively), the inactive α-ergocryptine (compound '14') and bromocriptine (compound' 19) which acted as a potent blocker (IC50 = 1.6 ± 0.4 µM) of Sm.5HTRL (Figure 3D).
evidence: This quantifies the agonist activity of ergotamine at all three receptors.

claim: Bromocriptine acted as a potent blocker of Sm.5HTRL (IC50 = 1.6 ± 0.4 µM).
source: Distinct structural modifications impacting efficacy could be seen in an ergopeptine series (Figure 3D), through comparison of the chemical structures of ergotamine (compound '1'), a potent full agonist at each schistosome receptor (Emax95 ± 4, 96 ± 5 and 114 ± 3% of 5-HT for Sm.5HTRL, Sh.5HTR and Sj.5HTR, respectively), the inactive α-ergocryptine (compound '14') and bromocriptine (compound' 19) which acted as a potent blocker (IC50 = 1.6 ± 0.4 µM) of Sm.5HTRL (Figure 3D).
evidence: This quantifies the antagonist potency of bromocriptine.

claim: Male and female schistosomes respond to 5-HT with increased movement.
source: Male and female worms respond to 5-HT with increased movement (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the ex vivo response of worms to serotonin, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Compounds that exhibited agonist activity at each of the three 5-HTRs in vitro also stimulated worm movement ex vivo.
source: Compounds that exhibited agonist activity at each of the three 5-HTRs in vitro also stimulated worm movement ex vivo (Figure 4C).
evidence: This validates the in vitro findings with ex vivo data, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ergot alkaloids displayed increased potency relative to 5-HT in stimulating worm movement (EC50 for 5-HT = 51.6 ± 3.0 µM, EC50 = 97.8 ± 31.6 nM for ergotamine, EC50 = 1.4 ± 0.5 µM for LSD).
source: While the rank order of potency varied slightly from the in vitro screen, an increase in potency of ergot alkaloids relative to 5-HT was evident (EC50 for 5-HT = 51.6 ± 3.0 µM, EC50 = 97.8 ± 31.6 nM for ergotamine, EC50 = 1.4 ± 0.5 µM for LSD).
evidence: This quantifies the potency of compounds in the ex vivo assay.

claim: BOL-148 blocked 5-HT evoked hyperactivity in schistosomes.
source: As expected, the potent antagonist BOL-148 (Figure 3C) blocked 5-HT evoked hyperactivity (Figure 4D).
evidence: This describes the antagonist activity of BOL-148 ex vivo, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: BOL-148 displayed approximately 10 fold higher potency than bromocriptine in blocking 5-HT evoked movement (IC50 = 28.8 ± 23.1 nM for BOL-148 versus IC50 = 331 ± 271 nM for bromocriptine).
source: BOL-148 displayed ~10 fold higher potency than bromocriptine consistent with the results from the in vitro screen (IC50 = 28.8 ± 23.1 nM for BOL-148 versus IC50 = 331 ± 271 nM for bromocriptine, Figure 4D).
evidence: This compares the potency of two antagonists ex vivo, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Processes such as parasite feeding, mate pairing and movement within the host vasculature depend upon coordinated neuromuscular function.
source: As processes such as parasite feeding, mate pairing and movement within the host vasculature depend upon coordinated neuromuscular function, exposure to ligands that stimulate hyperactivity (5-HTR agonists) or cause paralysis (5-HTR antagonists) may promote dysfunction and parasite clearance.
evidence: This provides rationale for targeting neuromuscular function.

claim: A hepatic shift of parasites from the mesenteric vessels to the liver is an indicator of acute drug efficacy that may prove indicative of anthelmintic activity.
source: One indicator of acute drug efficacy that may prove indicative of anthelmintic activity is a shift in location of the parasites from the mesenteric vessels to the liver (the 'hepatic shift'), where worms are subsequently targeted for elimination by the host immune system (Buttle and Khayyal, 1962; Pellegrino et al., 1977; Mehlhorn et al., 1981).
evidence: This describes a known indicator of drug efficacy, supported by citations.

claim: Following treatment with PZQ (100 mg/kg), most worms were found within the liver (68.8 ± 14.1% of recovered parasites).
source: Following treatment with PZQ (100 mg/kg), most of the worms were found within the liver (68.8 ± 14.1% of recovered parasites, Figure 5B), whereas worms were infrequently found within the liver in mice injected with vehicle control (9.7 ± 8.5% of recovered parasites).
evidence: This quantifies the hepatic shift caused by PZQ, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Worms were infrequently found within the liver in mice injected with vehicle control (9.7 ± 8.5% of recovered parasites).
source: Following treatment with PZQ (100 mg/kg), most of the worms were found within the liver (68.8 ± 14.1% of recovered parasites, Figure 5B), whereas worms were infrequently found within the liver in mice injected with vehicle control (9.7 ± 8.5% of recovered parasites).
evidence: This provides the baseline worm distribution in control animals.

claim: Treatment with 5-HTR agonists elicited a hepatic shift.
source: Treatment with 5-HTR agonists elicited a hepatic shift (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes the in vivo effect of agonists, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Treatment with 5-HTR antagonists did not alter worm distribution.
source: However, treatment with 5-HTR antagonists did not alter worm distribution (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes the lack of effect of antagonists in vivo, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The extent of the hepatic shift observed in mice treated with 5-HTR agonists correlated with the measured efficacy of these agonists at the parasite 5-HTR.
source: Furthermore, the extent of the hepatic shift observed in mice treated with 5-HTR agonists correlated with the measured efficacy of these agonists at the parasite 5.HTR (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes a correlation between in vitro and in vivo efficacy, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ergotamine treatment of mice yielded a similar percentage of worms in the liver (75.1 ± 16.9%) as seen in mice treated with PZQ.
source: Full agonists promoted the greatest shift: for example, ergotamine treatment of mice yielded a similar percentage of worms in the liver (75.1 ± 16.9%) as seen in mice treated with PZQ.
evidence: This compares the efficacy of ergotamine to PZQ in causing hepatic shift.

claim: Neither bromocriptine (2.0 ± 2.8% of worms in liver) nor BOL-148 (5.2 ± 2.3% of worms in liver) caused a hepatic shift of worms.
source: For example, neither bromocriptine (2.0 ± 2.8% of worms in liver) or BOL-148 (5.2 ± 2.3% of worms in liver) caused a hepatic shift of worms (Figure 5B) despite the effectiveness of these compounds at arresting worm movement ex vivo (Figure 4D).
evidence: This quantifies the lack of hepatic shift with antagonists, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Control animals succumbed to schistosome infection over a timeframe consistent with the onset of egg laying by sexually mature parasites (~8–10 weeks post infection).
source: Control animals succumbed to infection (~8–10 weeks p.i.) over a timeframe consistent with the onset of egg laying by sexually mature parasites as expected (Figure 6A, [Cheever, 1969]).
evidence: This describes the natural course of infection in control mice, shown in Figure 6A and supported by citation.

claim: By 15 weeks post infection, the majority of control mice were dead.
source: By 15 weeks p.i., the majority of control mice were dead.
evidence: This describes the mortality in control animals.

claim: Death rates were significantly reduced in ergotamine-treated mice (16.5% versus 68.9% mortality in control cohort, log-rank test p<0.001, hazard ratio 5.02).
source: Death rates were significantly reduced in ergotamine-treated mice (16.5% versus 68.9% mortality in control cohort, log-rank test p<0.001, hazard ratio 5.02).
evidence: This quantifies the survival benefit of ergotamine treatment with statistical analysis.

claim: PZQ-treated mice survived through 15 weeks with no observed lethality.
source: PZQ-treated mice survived through 15 weeks with no observed lethality (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes the complete survival of PZQ-treated mice, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ergotamine treatment significantly reduced worm burden from 28 ± 8 worm pairs per mouse to 9 ± 6 worm pairs per mouse (~65% reduction, p<0.002).
source: First, ergotamine treatment significantly reduced worm burden from 28 ± 8 worm pairs per mouse to 9 ± 6 worm pairs per mouse (~65% reduction, p<0.002; Figure 6B).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of ergotamine on worm burden with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Treatment with either ergotamine or PZQ resulted in a considerable reduction (96.3 ± 1.2 and 99.9 ± 0.1%, respectively) in intestinal egg burden.
source: Control mice contained large numbers of viable eggs in both the small and large intestine. However, treatment with either ergotamine or PZQ resulted in a considerable reduction (96.3 ± 1.2 and 99.9 ± 0.1%, respectively) in intestinal egg burden (Figure 6C).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of drugs on egg burden, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Egg laying was decreased following treatment with ergotamine (1 µM, 54.2 ± 12.6% reduction), serotonin (100 µM, 82.4 ± 2.2% reduction) or forskolin (100 µM, 61.6 ± 12.6% reduction).
source: Egg laying was decreased following treatment with ergotamine (1 µM, 54.2 ± 12.6% reduction), serotonin (100 µM, 82.4 ± 2.2% reduction) or forskolin (100 µM, 61.6 ± 12.6% reduction) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B&C).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of compounds on egg laying ex vivo, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Eggs laid by ergotamine treated worms were often small and deformed, indicating abnormal development.
source: Eggs laid by ergotamine treated worms were often small and deformed, indicating abnormal development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes morphological changes in eggs from treated worms, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Hepatosplenomegaly is a hallmark of chronic schistosomiasis.
source: Hepatosplenomegaly is a hallmark of chronic schistosomiasis and splenomegaly and liver fibrosis are observed in the murine model (Fallon, 2000).
evidence: This describes a characteristic pathological feature of schistosomiasis, supported by citation.

claim: Splenomegaly and liver fibrosis are observed in the murine model of schistosomiasis.
source: Hepatosplenomegaly is a hallmark of chronic schistosomiasis and splenomegaly and liver fibrosis are observed in the murine model (Fallon, 2000).
evidence: This describes pathological features in the mouse model, supported by citation.

claim: Uninfected mouse spleens weighed 0.12 ± 0.02 g while infected mouse spleens showed approximately 6 fold enlargement, weighing 0.76 ± 0.20 g at 49 days post infection.
source: This is reflected by comparison of the weights of uninfected mouse spleens (0.12 ± 0.02 g) and the spleens of infected littermates (~6 fold enlargement, weighing 0.76 ± 0.20 g at 49 days p.i), or increases in liver mass (~2 fold enlargement from 2.0 ± 0.3 g in uninfected mice to 4.8 ± 0.8 g in infected mice, Figure 6D).
evidence: This quantifies splenomegaly in infected mice, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Liver mass showed approximately 2 fold enlargement from 2.0 ± 0.3 g in uninfected mice to 4.8 ± 0.8 g in infected mice.
source: This is reflected by comparison of the weights of uninfected mouse spleens (0.12 ± 0.02 g) and the spleens of infected littermates (~6 fold enlargement, weighing 0.76 ± 0.20 g at 49 days p.i), or increases in liver mass (~2 fold enlargement from 2.0 ± 0.3 g in uninfected mice to 4.8 ± 0.8 g in infected mice, Figure 6D).
evidence: This quantifies hepatomegaly in infected mice, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PZQ treatment (one week, starting at 42 days post infection) did not prevent spleen and liver enlargement.
source: PZQ treatment (one week, starting at 42 days p.i) did not prevent spleen and liver enlargement (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes the lack of effect of PZQ on hepatosplenomegaly, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was no difference in the weights of the liver and spleen between PZQ-treated and vehicle treated infected mice.
source: There was no difference in the weights of the liver and spleen between PZQ-treated and vehicle treated infected mice (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This quantifies the lack of effect of PZQ on organ weights, shown in Figures 6E and F.

claim: PZQ is highly effective at eliminating worms at six weeks infection and beyond.
source: This is likely due to the fact that, while PZQ is highly effective at eliminating worms at six weeks infection and beyond (Sabah et al., 1986; Keiser et al., 2009), sexual maturation and egg laying commence as early as 5 weeks post infection (Sabah et al., 1986), meaning that eggs deposited prior to treatment initiation still evoke an immune response which PZQ exposure does not ameliorate.
evidence: This explains the timing of PZQ efficacy, supported by citations.

claim: Sexual maturation and egg laying in schistosomes commence as early as 5 weeks post infection.
source: This is likely due to the fact that, while PZQ is highly effective at eliminating worms at six weeks infection and beyond (Sabah et al., 1986; Keiser et al., 2009), sexual maturation and egg laying commence as early as 5 weeks post infection (Sabah et al., 1986), meaning that eggs deposited prior to treatment initiation still evoke an immune response which PZQ exposure does not ameliorate.
evidence: This describes the timing of parasite development, supported by citation.

claim: Ergotamine exposure prevented hepatosplenomegaly.
source: In contrast to PZQ, ergotamine exposure prevented hepatosplenomegaly.
evidence: This describes a unique effect of ergotamine compared to PZQ.

claim: Ergotamine reduced the infection-promoted increase in spleen mass by 55.8 ± 14.0% and liver mass by 52.0 ± 14.2% relative to vehicle treated controls.
source: Ergotamine reduced the infection-promoted increase in spleen mass by 55.8 ± 14.0% and liver mass by 52.0 ± 14.2% relative to vehicle treated controls (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of ergotamine on hepatosplenomegaly, shown in Figures 6E and F.

claim: Liver sections from ergotamine-treated infections displayed decreased granuloma formation and fibrosis.
source: Similarly, liver sections from ergotamine-treated infections displayed decreased granuloma formation and fibrosis when investigated by various staining methods (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes histological findings, shown in Figure 6G and supplementary figure.

claim: Movat's stain and Masson's trichrome showed decreased levels of collagen deposition surrounding granulomas in ergotamine-treated mice.
source: Movat's stain and Masson's trichrome showed decreased levels of collagen deposition surrounding granulomas (Figure 6G,II–III).
evidence: This describes specific histological findings, shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Aldehyde fuchsin stain showed elastin surrounding the granulomas of DMSO and PZQ treated mice, while the livers of uninfected or ergotamine treated mice exhibited little staining.
source: Aldehyde fuchsin stain showed elastin surrounding the granulomas of DMSO and PZQ treated mice, while the livers of uninfected or ergotamine treated mice exhibited little staining (Figure 6G,IV).
evidence: This describes elastin staining patterns, shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Oil red O staining revealed lipid stores present in the livers of uninfected mice that were absent in infected control livers.
source: Oil red O staining revealed lipid stores present in the livers of uninfected mice that were absent in infected control livers.
evidence: This describes lipid staining patterns in different groups.

claim: Treatment with ergotamine, but not PZQ, preserved regions of Oil red O positive staining - albeit at lower levels than healthy livers.
source: Treatment with ergotamine, but not PZQ, preserved regions of Oil red O positive staining - albeit at lower levels than healthy livers (Figure 6G,V).
evidence: This describes a unique effect of ergotamine on lipid preservation, shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Pro-apoptotic cleaved caspase-3 was present in cells within granulomas of all three infected livers (DMSO control, ergotamine and PZQ treated).
source: Pro-apoptotic cleaved caspase-3 was present in cells within granulomas of all three infected livers (DMSO control, ergotamine and PZQ treated – Figure 6G,VI).
evidence: This describes caspase-3 staining patterns, shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Both 5-HT and ergotamine stimulated movement of juvenile worms ex vivo.
source: Both 5-HT and ergotamine stimulated movement of juvenile worms ex vivo (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This describes the effect of compounds on immature worms, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Early dosing with ergotamine prior to egg laying (3–4 weeks post infection) did not resolve infections, mirroring the lack of effect of PZQ.
source: In vivo, however, early dosing with ergotamine prior to egg laying (3–4 weeks post infection) did not resolve infections, mirroring the lack of effect of PZQ (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This describes the lack of efficacy of ergotamine against immature infections, shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Ergotamine was highly effective at promoting survival in mice with mature infections through reductions in worm and egg number.
source: In conclusion, these data show that ergotamine was highly effective at promoting survival in mice with mature infections (Figure 6A) through reductions in worm (Figure 6B) and egg number (Figure 6C).
evidence: This summarizes the efficacy of ergotamine, referencing multiple figures.

claim: Unlike PZQ, ergotamine was effective at attenuating hepatosplenomegaly associated with the chronic pathology of schistosomiasis.
source: However - unlike PZQ - ergotamine was effective at attenuating hepatosplenomegaly associated with the chronic pathology of schistosomiasis.
evidence: This highlights a unique property of ergotamine compared to PZQ.

claim: Ergotamine is a human therapeutic with affinity for various host GPCRs.
source: As ergotamine is a human therapeutic with affinity for various host GPCRs (O'Connor and Roth, 2005), in addition to high affinity for schistosome 5-HT receptors (Figure 3D), engagement of host signaling pathways likely underpins these protective effects.
evidence: This describes the polypharmacology of ergotamine, supported by citation.

claim: Engagement of host signaling pathways likely underpins the protective effects of ergotamine.
source: As ergotamine is a human therapeutic with affinity for various host GPCRs (O'Connor and Roth, 2005), in addition to high affinity for schistosome 5-HT receptors (Figure 3D), engagement of host signaling pathways likely underpins these protective effects.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of ergotamine's protective effects.

claim: RNA-Seq analyses were performed on the livers and spleens of schistosome-infected mice following drug treatment over a window 6 to 7 weeks post-infection.
source: To investigate mechanisms contributing to the differential in vivo effects of these drugs, we performed RNA-Seq analyses on the livers and spleens of schistosome-infected mice following drug treatment (PZQ, ergotamine) over a window 6 to 7 weeks post-infection (Figure 7A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for transcriptomic analysis, shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Of the 24,421 transcripts with mapped sequencing reads, 9684 transcripts were differentially expressed in infected livers and 7325 transcripts were differentially expressed in infected spleens.
source: Livers and spleens of infected mice showed widespread changes in gene expression relative to uninfected littermates; of the 24,421 transcripts with mapped sequencing reads, 9684 transcripts were differentially expressed in infected livers and 7325 transcripts were differentially expressed in infected spleens.
evidence: This quantifies the transcriptional changes with infection.

claim: The host pathology of schistosomiasis infection is driven by an initial Th1 response to the worms themselves followed by a sustained Th2 response that drives egg-induced fibrosis.
source: It is well established that the host pathology of schistosomiasis infection is driven by an initial Th1 response to the worms themselves followed by a sustained Th2 response that drives egg-induced fibrosis (reviewed in [Pearce and MacDonald, 2002; Wynn et al., 2004]).
evidence: This describes the immunological basis of schistosomiasis pathology, supported by citations.

claim: Most components of Th1 and Th2 signaling pathways were significantly changed in both infected livers and spleens relative to uninfected littermates.
source: Most components of Th1 and Th2 signaling pathways were significantly changed in both infected livers and spleens relative to uninfected littermates (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This describes transcriptional changes in immune pathways, shown in Figures 7B and C.

claim: Drug treatment with either PZQ or ergotamine attenuated transcriptional changes associated with infection.
source: Drug treatment with either PZQ or ergotamine attenuated transcriptional changes associated with infection.
evidence: This describes the general effect of drug treatment on gene expression.

claim: PZQ or ergotamine treatment decreased expression of pathways associated with host immune response to either parasites or bacteria entering the circulation.
source: Specifically, PZQ or ergotamine treatment decreased expression of pathways associated with host immune response to either parasites (acute phase response signaling, Th1 and Th2 pathway) or bacteria entering the circulation with the breakdown of the intestinal epithelium that occurs with heavy parasite egg production ultimately leading to host death (LPS/IL-1 mediated inhibition of RXR function [Feingold et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2005]).
evidence: This describes specific pathway changes with drug treatment, supported by citations.

claim: Expression of pathways associated with drug metabolism and liver function increased with both PZQ and ergotamine treatments.
source: Expression of pathways associated with drug metabolism (xenobiotic metabolism signaling) and liver function (hepatic cholestasis) increased with both treatments (Figure 7D).
evidence: This describes pathway changes with drug treatment, shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The PZQ and ergotamine cohorts shared similar transcriptional patterns relative to control infection, consistent with both treatments resolving infection and parasite egg production.
source: These observations that the PZQ and ergotamine cohorts shared similar transcriptional patterns relative to control infection is consistent with both treatments resolving infection and parasite egg production (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This interprets the transcriptional data in the context of efficacy data.

claim: Ingenuity pathway analysis using triple-filtered criteria identified a cohort of transcripts uniquely associated with ergotamine, but not PZQ, treatment that were tagged for involvement in hepatic fibrosis and hepatic stellate cell activation (p-value 0.00015, Fisher's exact test).
source: Ingenuity pathway analysis using this triple-filtered criteria identified a cohort of transcripts uniquely associated with ergotamine, but not PZQ, treatment. These transcripts were tagged for involvement in hepatic fibrosis and hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation (p-value 0.00015, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This describes pathway analysis results with statistical significance.

claim: Ergotamine treatment down-regulated gene products associated with HSC activation relative to control infections, while PZQ treatment had little to no effect on the same suite of transcripts.
source: Ergotamine treatment down-regulated gene products associated with HSC activation to control infections, while PZQ treatment had little to no effect on the same suite of transcripts.
evidence: This describes differential effects of the two drugs on HSC-related genes.

claim: Hepatic stellate cells represent a quiescent, non-proliferative cell population in normal liver but once activated during injury or disease, drive fibrotic responses by transforming into proliferative, contractile myofibroblasts that deposit extracellular matrix components.
source: HSCs represent a quiescent, non-proliferative cell population in normal liver but once activated during injury or disease, drive fibrotic responses by transforming into proliferative, contractile myofibroblasts that deposit extracellular matrix components (Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017).
evidence: This describes the biology of hepatic stellate cells, supported by citation.

claim: Differentially expressed transcripts in ergotamine-treated samples included known markers of HSC activation responsible for extracellular matrix production, contraction, migration, survival and transdifferentiation into myofibroblasts.
source: Differentially expressed transcripts in ergotamine-treated samples (Supplementary file 4) included known markers of HSC activation responsible for extracellular matrix production (COL1A1, COL1A2, COL3A1), transcripts associated with HSC contraction (CACNA1E, CACNA1H), migration (IGFBP3, RANTES), survival (IGFBP5, GAS6) and transdifferentiation into myofibroblasts (MMP13, GLI1, PAK1) (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This lists specific genes affected by ergotamine treatment, shown in Figures 7F and G.

claim: Ligands that control HSC activation and survival were also differentially expressed (PDGFB, IL13RA2, BMP4, IL-4, SAA).
source: Ligands that control HSC activation and survival were also differentially expressed (PDGFB, IL13RA2, BMP4, IL-4, SAA).
evidence: This lists additional genes affected by ergotamine treatment.

claim: Ergotamine and PZQ were both effective at promoting survival through reductions in worm and egg number, as well as reversing many transcriptional signatures that drive host pathological outcomes in response to parasite infection.
source: Therefore, ergotamine and PZQ were both effective at promoting survival (Figure 6A) through reductions in worm (Figure 6B) and egg number (Figure 6C), as well as reversing many transcriptional signatures that drive host pathological outcomes in response to parasite infection (Figure 7D).
evidence: This summarizes the shared effects of both drugs, referencing multiple figures.

claim: Unlike PZQ, ergotamine was effective at attenuating the hepatosplenomegaly associated with the chronic pathology of schistosomiasis due to decreased activation of profibrotic HSCs.
source: However, unlike PZQ, ergotamine was also effective at attenuating the hepatosplenomegaly associated with the chronic pathology of schistosomiasis (Figure 6D–G), due to decreased activation of profibrotic HSCs (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This summarizes the unique effect of ergotamine and its mechanism, referencing multiple figures.

claim: The possibility of serotonergic drugs providing effective antiparasitic agents has long been recognized.
source: Given the importance of serotonergic signaling in parasite physiology, the possibility of serotonergic drugs providing effective antiparasitic agents has long been recognized (Mansour, 1979).
evidence: This provides historical context, supported by citation.

claim: Ergotamine was first isolated 100 years ago.
source: This pipeline identified unique properties of ergotamine, an ergot alkaloid first isolated 100 years ago (Hofmann, 1978) and FDA-approved medication for migraine, for treating schistosomiasis.
evidence: This provides historical context for ergotamine, supported by citation.

claim: Ergotamine is an FDA-approved medication for migraine.
source: This pipeline identified unique properties of ergotamine, an ergot alkaloid first isolated 100 years ago (Hofmann, 1978) and FDA-approved medication for migraine, for treating schistosomiasis.
evidence: This describes the current clinical use of ergotamine.

claim: Ergotamine increased survival in a murine model of schistosomiasis through reductions in parasite burden and resultant egg load, but most intriguingly resolved inflammatory damage caused by schistosome eggs laid in host tissues, an effect not observed with PZQ under the same conditions.
source: Ergotamine increased survival in a murine model of schistosomiasis through reductions in parasite burden and resultant egg load, but most intriguingly resolved inflammatory damage caused by schistosome eggs laid in host tissues, an effect not observed with PZQ under the same conditions (Figure 6).
evidence: This summarizes the key findings of the study, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The effects of ergotamine likely result from the broad polypharmacology that coalesces a fortuitous combination of effects at both host and parasite GPCRs.
source: These effects likely result from the broad polypharmacology of ergotamine that coalesces a fortuitous combination of effects at both host and parasite GPCRs.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying ergotamine's unique efficacy.

claim: Ergotamine is a potent Sm.5HTRL agonist.
source: Ergotamine is a potent Sm.5HTRL agonist (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the pharmacological activity of ergotamine, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sm.5HTRL and homologs of this receptor in other flatworms regulate movement.
source: Sm.5HTRL and homologs of this receptor in other flatworms, regulate movement (Patocka et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the function of the receptor, supported by citations.

claim: Sm.5HTRL is downregulated upon pairing of adult S. mansoni females and males, implicating an additional role in sexual maturation.
source: Sm.5HTRL is downregulated upon pairing of adult S. mansoni females and males, implicating an additional role in sexual maturation (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes expression changes of the receptor, supported by citation.

claim: As a Gs coupled receptor, the role of 5-HT acting through cAMP to regulate flatworm metabolism is relevant.
source: As a Gs coupled receptor, the role of 5-HT acting through cAMP to regulate flatworm metabolism is also relevant (Mansour, 1984).
evidence: This describes the signaling mechanism and physiological role, supported by citation.

claim: The broad physiological roles of Sm.5HTRL - motor function, female egg production, metabolism – underscore consideration of Sm.5HTRL as an attractive antischistosomal target.
source: These broad physiological roles - motor function, female egg production, metabolism – underscore consideration of Sm.5HTRL as an attractive antischistosomal target.
evidence: This is an inference about the value of the target based on its multiple roles.

claim: Structure-activity studies confirmed the ergoline core as a customizable scaffold for ligand optimization at Sm.5HTRL.
source: Screening hits (Figure 2), and subsequent structure-activity studies (Figure 3) confirmed the ergoline core as a customizable scaffold for ligand optimization at Sm.5HTRL.
evidence: This summarizes the SAR findings, referencing Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Sm.5HTRL agonists and antagonists stimulated and inhibited adult worm motility ex vivo as predicted.
source: These analyses provided a toolbox of compounds with varied potencies and efficacies against Sm.5HTRLin vitro and Sm.5HTRL agonists and antagonists stimulated and inhibited adult worm motility ex vivo as predicted (Figure 4).
evidence: This validates the in vitro findings with ex vivo data, shown in Figure 4.

claim: In vivo, only agonists of Sm.5HTRL signaling caused a hepatic shift of worms and mitigated worm burden, while Sm.5HTRL blockers were ineffective.
source: However in vivo, only agonists of Sm.5HTRL signaling caused a hepatic shift of worms and mitigated worm burden, Sm.5HTRL blockers were ineffective (Figure 5).
evidence: This describes the differential in vivo efficacy of agonists versus antagonists, shown in Figure 5.

claim: The observation that only agonists were effective in vivo was surprising given the presumed beneficial effect of causing potent or long-lasting worm paralysis.
source: This observation was surprising given the presumed beneficial effect of causing potent (BOL-148) or long-lasting (bromocriptine) worm paralysis (Chan et al., 2016a, 2016c), but nevertheless informative for future phenotypic screens to prioritize 'hyperactive' over 'hypoactive' serotoninergic hits.
evidence: This expresses surprise at the finding and draws implications for future screening, supported by citations.

claim: Ergotamine acts as a vasoconstrictor, including within the mesenteric vasculature where the adult worms reside.
source: Acutely, ergotamine acts as a vasoconstrictor, including within the mesenteric vasculature where the adult worms reside (Mikkelsen et al., 1981).
evidence: This describes a known pharmacological effect of ergotamine, supported by citation.

claim: Disruption of the parasite environment consequent to ergotamine-evoked mechanical changes and alterations of blood flow within the hepatic portal system could drive parasites from the mesenteries to the liver for elimination.
source: Disruption of the parasite environment consequent to ergotamine-evoked mechanical changes and alterations of blood flow within the hepatic portal system could drive parasites from the mesenteries to the liver for elimination.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism for how ergotamine causes hepatic shift.

claim: R-PZQ acts as a human 5-HT2B receptor partial agonist that contracts host mesenteric vessels.
source: This action would mirror recent data demonstrating R-PZQ, which also causes a hepatic shift, acts a human 5-HT2B receptor partial agonist that contracts host mesenteric vessels (Chan et al., 2017).
evidence: This provides a parallel mechanism for PZQ, supported by citation.

claim: Drug treatment with either PZQ or ergotamine improved various aspects of liver function relative to untreated infections.
source: Chronically, drug treatment with either PZQ or ergotamine improved various aspects of liver function (hepatic cholestasis, retinol metabolism, bile acid synthesis, Figure 7D and Supplementary file 4) relative to untreated infections.
evidence: This describes transcriptional changes indicating improved liver function, shown in Figure 7D and supplementary file.

claim: Beneficial changes highlighted by RNA-Seq encompassed protection against intestinal damage.
source: Beneficial changes highlighted by RNA-Seq also encompassed protection against intestinal damage (Cao et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes additional beneficial effects observed in the transcriptional data, supported by citation.

claim: Various pathways involved in response to bacterial infection were down regulated with PZQ and ergotamine treatment relative to control infections.
source: Various pathways involved in response to bacterial infection were down regulated with PZQ and ergotamine treatment relative to control infections (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This describes transcriptional changes in pathways related to bacterial infection.

claim: Mice experience a relative infection burden orders of magnitude higher than typical for humans.
source: This is likely because mice experience a relative infection burden orders of magnitude higher than typical for humans (Cheever, 1969) resulting in compromised intestinal integrity and release of microbiota into the circulation as mature parasites commence egg production.
evidence: This explains differences between mouse and human infections, supported by citation.

claim: Ergotamine additionally provided protection against the spleen and liver enlargement that persisted in PZQ-treated mice, suggesting a further action of ergotamine on the host immune response.
source: However, ergotamine additionally provided protection against the spleen and liver enlargement that persisted in PZQ-treated mice (Figure 6D and E), suggesting a further action of ergotamine on the host immune response.
evidence: This highlights a unique effect of ergotamine and infers a mechanism, shown in Figures 6D and E.

claim: Hepatic stellate cells are key drivers of fibrosis during liver disease.
source: Hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) are key drivers of fibrosis during liver disease.
evidence: This describes the role of HSCs in liver pathology.

claim: Upon their transformation into myofibroblasts, HSCs initiate active production of extracellular matrix components and decrease lipid storage.
source: Upon their transformation into myofibroblasts, HSCs initiate active production of extracellular matrix components (collagen, elastin – Figure 6G,II-IV) and decrease lipid storage (Figure 6G,V, [Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017]).
evidence: This describes the functional changes in activated HSCs, shown in Figure 6G and supported by citation.

claim: HSCs express a portfolio of GPCRs that regulate activation and transformation.
source: HSCs are known to express a portfolio of GPCRs that regulate activation and transformation (Tsuchida and Friedman, 2017).
evidence: This describes the GPCR expression profile of HSCs, supported by citation.

claim: HSCs express several serotonergic GPCRs (5HT1B, 5HT1F, 5HT2A, 5HT2B, 5HT7).
source: These include several serotonergic GPCRs (5HT1B, 5HT1F, 5HT2A, 5HT2B, 5HT7, [Ruddell et al., 2006]).
evidence: This lists specific serotonergic receptors expressed by HSCs, supported by citation.

claim: The known polypharmacological signature of ergotamine closely matches the serotoninergic GPCR expression profile in HSCs.
source: It is tantalizing that the known polypharmacological signature of ergotamine (O'Connor and Roth, 2005) closely matches the serotoninergic GPCR expression profile in HSCs (Ruddell et al., 2006).
evidence: This notes a correspondence between ergotamine's targets and HSC receptor expression, supported by citations.

claim: The correspondence between ergotamine's polypharmacology and HSC receptor expression may imply a cell-autonomous action of ergotamine on HSCs.
source: This may imply a cell-autonomous action of ergotamine on HSCs, although further insight would be needed to distinguish this possibility from non cell-autonomous mechanisms given that serotonin impacts immune responses and liver regeneration in a multiplicity of ways (Herr et al., 2017; Lesurtel et al., 2006; Ebrahimkhani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism that requires further investigation, supported by citations.

claim: Ergotamine could impair HSCs indirectly by inhibiting macrophage polarization or immune mediators such as TNF-α and ICAM-1.
source: For example, ergotamine could impair HSCs indirectly by inhibiting macrophage polarization (de las Casas-Engel et al., 2013) or immune mediators such as TNF-α and ICAM-1 (54).
evidence: This proposes alternative mechanisms for ergotamine's effects, supported by citation.

claim: ICAM-1 is found at elevated levels within egg-evoked granulomas.
source: ICAM-1 is found at elevated levels within egg-evoked granulomas (Ritter and McKerrow, 1996) and TNF-α drives the host immune response to schistosome eggs (Amiri et al., 1992; Leptak and McKerrow, 1997).
evidence: This describes the role of ICAM-1 in granulomas, supported by citation.

claim: TNF-α drives the host immune response to schistosome eggs.
source: ICAM-1 is found at elevated levels within egg-evoked granulomas (Ritter and McKerrow, 1996) and TNF-α drives the host immune response to schistosome eggs (Amiri et al., 1992; Leptak and McKerrow, 1997).
evidence: This describes the role of TNF-α in the immune response, supported by citations.

claim: T-cell deprived mice exhibit hepatic microvesicular steatosis, since granulomas also have a beneficial function of facilitating excretion of eggs from the mesenteries and sequestering toxic egg products.
source: Prior studies on schistosome infection of immune compromised mice have shown that T-cell deprived mice exhibit hepatic microvesicular steatosis, since granulomas also have a beneficial function of facilitating excretion of eggs from the mesenteries and sequestering toxic egg products (reviewed in [Hams et al., 2013; Doenhoff et al., 1986]).
evidence: This describes findings from immune-compromised mice, supported by citations.

claim: Ergotamine treatment impaired the granulomatous response to eggs, but increased microvascular damage was not observed.
source: Ergotamine treatment impaired the granulomatous response to eggs (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), but increased microvascular damage was not observed (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the effect of ergotamine on granulomas without causing additional damage, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The polypharmacology of ergotamine evidences the principle of combining host and parasite responses for therapeutic effect.
source: While the polypharmacology of ergotamine evidences the principle of combining host and parasite responses for therapeutic effect, it is not itself a likely candidate for repurposing.
evidence: This draws a general conclusion about the therapeutic strategy while noting limitations of ergotamine itself.

claim: Ergotamine is not itself a likely candidate for repurposing as an antischistosomal drug.
source: While the polypharmacology of ergotamine evidences the principle of combining host and parasite responses for therapeutic effect, it is not itself a likely candidate for repurposing.
evidence: This states a limitation of ergotamine for clinical development.

claim: Repeated dosing of ergotamine as an antimigraine therapy is associated with known side effects.
source: Repeated dosing of ergotamine as an antimigraine therapy is associated with known side effects: it is contraindicated in pregnancy and poorly suited for the large pediatric population susceptible to schistosomiasis.
evidence: This describes safety concerns with ergotamine.

claim: Ergotamine is contraindicated in pregnancy.
source: Repeated dosing of ergotamine as an antimigraine therapy is associated with known side effects: it is contraindicated in pregnancy and poorly suited for the large pediatric population susceptible to schistosomiasis.
evidence: This states a specific contraindication for ergotamine.

claim: Ergotamine is poorly suited for the large pediatric population susceptible to schistosomiasis.
source: Repeated dosing of ergotamine as an antimigraine therapy is associated with known side effects: it is contraindicated in pregnancy and poorly suited for the large pediatric population susceptible to schistosomiasis.
evidence: This identifies a limitation for using ergotamine in the target population.

claim: For future studies, analogs with improved pharmacokinetic profile and bioavailability will need to be evaluated for clinical potential as safe and effective agents.
source: For future studies, analogs with improved pharmacokinetic profile and bioavailability will need to be evaluated for clinical potential as safe and effective agents.
evidence: This proposes a direction for future drug development.

claim: For treatment of parasitic infections, a single bolus dose may provide more flexibility and avoid cumulative side effects associated with repeated dosing.
source: Indeed, for treatment of parasitic infections, a single bolus dose may provide more flexibility and avoid cumulative side effects associated with repeated dosing.
evidence: This proposes an alternative dosing strategy.

claim: Limited structural-activity studies suggest modifications of the core ergot alkaloid scaffold can generate analogs with a range of potencies and efficacy.
source: Our limited structural-activity studies to date (e.g. Figure 3) on schistosome GPCRs do suggest modifications of the core ergot alkaloid scaffold can generate analogs with a range of potencies and efficacy.
evidence: This draws a conclusion from the SAR data about the potential for analog development, referencing Figure 3.

claim: Ergotamine is fortuitously suited to engage pathways in both host and parasite that are simultaneously deleterious to the blood fluke but beneficial to the infected host in terms of worm clearance and mitigation of damage caused by eggs.
source: In conclusion, ergotamine is fortuitously suited to engage pathways in both host and parasite that are simultaneously deleterious to the blood fluke but beneficial to the infected host in terms of worm clearance and mitigation of damage caused by eggs.
evidence: This summarizes the key finding of the study.

claim: Rather than prioritizing 'selective' antiparasitic therapies with no host effects, these data demonstrate merit in evaluating agents with broader polypharmacology across parasite and host as a route to discovering effective treatments for parasitic disease.
source: Rather than prioritizing 'selective' antiparasitic therapies with no host effects, these data demonstrate merit in evaluating agents with broader polypharmacology across parasite and host as a route to novel discovering effective treatments for parasitic disease.
evidence: This states the main conclusion and proposed paradigm shift for antiparasitic drug discovery.
